title: Leading Operational KPIs and the CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit

epigraph.quote: The successful completion of CCL Stage 3 and our continued debottlenecking efforts provide increased visibility into our initial production forecast for 2027.
epigraph.author: Jack Fusco, CEO, 2026 third-quarter release [3]

web_blocks.text: For an LNG exporter, revenue and net income are not enough. Track whether customer contracts come before new spending, whether trains meet build dates, whether gas and pipeline service reach the site, whether cargoes load on time and whether customers pay. Cheniere reports many of these measures. It does not publish a standard annual utilization rate for each train or a companywide DSO series. Those gaps matter. [2][3]

web_blocks.caption: Six operating KPIs to monitor ahead of reported cash flow
rows: 1. Cargoes and TBtu loaded / recognized
Throughput drives LNG sales and reveals whether physical output is reaching customers.
Q3 2026: 188 cargoes and 684 TBtu exported; nine months: 559 cargoes and 2,044 TBtu. Exported, loaded and recognized quantities differ when cargoes are in transit. [3]
2. Train commissioning and completion milestones
A train must progress from construction through first LNG and substantial completion before it contributes stable commercial output.

CCL Stage 3 was substantially complete on August 28, 2026, ahead of the guaranteed completion schedule and within budget according to the release. The CCL 8&9 project was 58.6% complete at September 30, with expected substantial completion in 2H 2028. [3]
3. Long-term contracted capacity and remaining term
Contracted volumes can underwrite project financing and create visibility before first production.

The 10-K describes a target of contracting about 90% of current and planned capacity and reports about 15 years of weighted-average remaining life for existing SPAs/IPM agreements at year-end 2025; specific contract economics remain confidential. [2]
4. Feed-gas and firm-transport access
The terminal cannot liquefy gas that cannot reach its inlet at the required rate.

Sabine Pass has multiple pipeline connections and Corpus Christi access includes Permian supply. Cheniere reports long-term transportation agreements but does not publish a consolidated procurement coverage percentage in the cited material. [2][4][5]
5. Delivery reliability, in-transit cargoes and customer credit
Missed deliveries, delivery timing and receivable aging can affect both trust and cash conversion.

The company reported 61 TBtu of delivered LNG in transit at September 30, 2026. One customer represented 15% of year-end 2025 trade receivables plus contract assets; a company-wide DSO measure is not disclosed. [2][3]
6. Expansion funding and permits before FID
Permitting, commercial commitments and financing should precede irreversible construction capital.

CCL Stage 4 remained in FERC review and unapproved; the first SPL Expansion phase's proposed term financing was subject to a positive FID and customary conditions. The 2026 Q3 release separated operating, under-construction and permitting capacity. [3][20]
web_blocks.takeaway: The KPIs link contract coverage and project gates to the physical throughput that ultimately generates cash; gaps in utilization and DSO disclosures should remain visible rather than be guessed.

web_blocks.title: CEO walk-the-talk audit: dated commitments versus outcomes

web_blocks.caption: A compact execution audit, separating delivered facts from open guidance
rows: 2010–2012: pivot Sabine Pass from import service to export; secure authorization and begin construction after a positive FID
First LNG cargo shipped in February 2016; Corpus Christi began LNG production in 2018; company history records continued train additions at both sites.
The strategic pivot was realized, though it required a long development and financing interval. [1]
2022: full notice to proceed on CCL Stage 3; complete the seven-train expansion within its contractual schedule and budget

First LNG from the first Stage 3 train was produced in December 2024; the seventh train reached substantial completion on August 28, 2026, ahead of guaranteed schedule and within budget per the company's release.
Strong project-delivery evidence. The on-budget and ahead-of-schedule assertion is company-reported; the completion milestone is dated and specific. [2][3][10]
2025: complete the 20/20 Vision capital-allocation plan and continue to fund disciplined growth
Cheniere reported the 20/20 Vision plan completed nearly a year ahead of schedule; 2026 nine-month growth capex was $2.8B, with $1.1B funded by equity cash flows.
The plan milestone is reported as delivered. The quality of future allocation still depends on project returns and actual funding requirements. [3][11]
2026 Q2: raise full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $7.90–$8.40B and DCF to $5.30–$5.80B
After Q3, management raised guidance again to Adjusted EBITDA of $8.75–$9.25B and DCF of $6.05–$6.55B. Nine-month 2026 Adjusted EBITDA was $6.037B and DCF was $4.07B.
The upward revision is consistent with management's stated operating outlook, but full-year guidance is not an audited outcome and DCF is non-GAAP. [3][9]
2026: advance future brownfield capacity while conditioning new capital on approvals, contracts and financing

Petrobras signed a 22-year 0.8 mtpa FOB SPA; QatarEnergy agreements cover up to 4 mtpa through 2054, with 1 mtpa contingent on an SPL Expansion FID. The first SPL phase had financing commitments conditional on FID; CCL Stage 4 remained under FERC review.
Commercial progress is concrete, but conditional volume and project permissions must not be treated as completed capacity or funded production. [3][20][13]
web_blocks.takeaway: The strongest recent evidence is physical completion and customer contracting. Guidance and permitting remain forward-looking until year-end results and regulatory decisions are known.

web_blocks.text: The latest concall tied completed execution to a still-unfinished forecast. CEO Jack Fusco said the completed CCL Stage 3 project and debottlenecking gave Cheniere "increased visibility into our initial production forecast for 2027." [3][8] That is visibility, not a delivered full-year result. CFO Zach Davis said the first phase of the Sabine Pass expansion was "well positioned to reach FID ... in the coming months, after receipt of final regulatory approvals." [8] The qualification is the most important part of the sentence: contracts and lender commitments help, but they do not replace an approved FID.

Management's preliminary 2027 plan is 56–58 million tonnes across both sites. About 52 million tonnes are expected under long-term contracts, and about 1 million tonnes remained unsold at the Q3 call. This volume outlook tests train availability and customer coverage; it is not financial guidance. Management said 2027 financial ranges would come with its February call. [8]

Jack Fusco said Stage 3 and debottlenecking improved visibility into 2027 production. Test that claim against actual output and cargoes. Allow for commissioning, maintenance, weather and gas limits. In the first nine months of 2026, exports rose 17% year over year and Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA rose 23%. GAAP net income fell because derivatives moved against Cheniere. These measures can point in different directions. [3]

The next capacity step should be audited with equal rigor. At Q3 2026 Cheniere described approximately 56 mtpa in operation, approximately 5 mtpa under construction or commissioning and more than 40 mtpa in permitting. The operating figure can anchor current throughput; the other two require different gates. Permitted capacity is not construction-ready capacity, and construction-ready capacity is not finished production. The conditional 1 mtpa portion of the QatarEnergy agreement should remain classified as conditional until the required FID and other conditions are satisfied. [3][20]

The six indicators should be read as a sequence rather than six independent scorecards. Contract coverage precedes FID; FID and financing precede full construction; pipeline availability and commissioning precede sustained cargoes; delivery, contract assets and collections follow the physical sale. A break early in the chain can appear later as unused construction capital or lower output. Cheniere's release gives concrete examples of each stage: long-term SPAs, project-completion percentages, completed trains, cargo totals and in-transit volumes. [2][3]

Safety and availability deserve a place beside capacity growth. A terminal outage, maintenance turnaround or weather event can interrupt a long-term delivery schedule and lower throughput even when customer demand is firm. The 10-K identifies production levels and maintenance timing as reasons operating profit may vary through the year, and the company describes safety and operational excellence as core priorities. The cited materials do not offer a unified train-level availability percentage, so cargo count and disclosed outage or commissioning commentary remain the public proxies rather than a synthetic utilization calculation. [2][3][4][5]

The operational dashboard should connect physical and commercial measures. If cargoes rise while contract assets or receivables rise faster, the explanation may be payment timing, delivered cargoes in transit or billing terms; the cited public material does not disclose enough to collapse those possibilities into one DSO statistic. If a project's completion percentage rises but customer commitments or funding remain conditional, the train's eventual cash contribution remains uncertain. The useful audit is to ask what changed at each gate and whether the next gate is supported by a dated filing or only by management expectation. [2][3][20]

The CEO's walk-the-talk record is strongest where a promise had a measurable finish line. The CCL Stage 3 schedule was followed from first LNG, through successive train completions, to the final August 2026 handover; management then reported the project ahead of the guaranteed schedule and within budget. The latest guidance revisions are less settled: management raised its ranges as nine-month volumes and Adjusted EBITDA improved, but audited full-year delivery remained pending. Preserve that distinction when assessing execution credibility. [2][3][9][10]

book_paragraphs: How can you know whether an LNG platform is improving before the financial statements show it? Start with the chain of leading indicators. A contract signed before an expansion reaches FID lowers the risk that new capacity has no buyer. A train's progress through engineering, procurement and construction tells you whether promised capacity is becoming physical. First LNG indicates the process equipment is operating, but substantial completion and dependable cargoes still matter. Loaded volume and recognized volume then show whether production is reaching the customer and whether the accounting transfer point has passed. [2][3]

The cargo count is an especially clear operating measure. Cheniere exported 188 cargoes and 684 TBtu in Q3 2026, and 559 cargoes and 2,044 TBtu in the first nine months. The comparison with 2025 showed volume growth. But don't confuse an exported cargo with revenue recognized in the same period: some delivered cargoes were still in transit at quarter-end. The same careful distinction applies to a train. A mechanical completion or first LNG milestone is progress, not proof of a full year at steady output. [3]

Commercial coverage is another lead. Cheniere describes a goal of contracting roughly 90% of current and planned capacity under long-term SPAs and IPM agreements, and it reported around 15 years of weighted-average remaining life at the end of 2025. The benefit is visibility: a project can be planned around expected sales. The limitation is that the specific contracts and prices are not fully public, and a contract can carry distinct cancellation, nomination, delivery and credit provisions. Petrobras's 0.8 mtpa, 22-year FOB agreement is one public example; it has no disclosed price in the release. [2][3]

Feed-gas availability should sit beside the contract book. Cheniere buys gas and arranges pipeline transport from a wide producer base. Sabine Pass is connected to multiple pipeline systems; Corpus Christi can access basins that include the Permian. The filings do not give a single companywide percentage for gas supply secured or a standardized utilization percentage by train. That missing data matters because high nameplate capacity does not guarantee operating throughput. You can still monitor cargo volumes, train availability and pipeline developments; you should not fill the disclosure gap with a guessed utilization figure. [2][4][5]

Now audit what management promised. The 2010–2012 export pivot became real: Sabine Pass shipped the first cargo in 2016 and Corpus Christi began production in 2018. This was a multiyear strategic bet rather than a quick operational adjustment. Later, the Stage 3 expansion received full notice to proceed in 2022; the first train produced LNG in December 2024, and the final train reached substantial completion in August 2026. Cheniere reported the project was completed ahead of its guaranteed schedule and within budget. That is strong evidence for the current execution team, although the schedule and budget description is management's own disclosure. [1][2][3][10]

The company's 20/20 Vision capital-allocation plan was reported complete nearly a year early. The broader promise was to balance debt strength, growth and shareholder returns. In the first nine months of 2026, Cheniere repurchased 7.7 million shares for $1.8 billion, paid dividends and invested $2.8 billion in growth projects, of which $1.1 billion was funded by equity cash flows. Those are actual deployments. Whether each growth dollar earns its intended return remains a separate long-horizon question, and the company does not provide a complete public project-by-project realized-return ledger. [3][11]

Finally, distinguish guidance from delivery. In August 2026, management raised its full-year guidance; after Q3 it raised it again. Nine-month adjusted EBITDA was $6.037 billion and DCF was $4.07 billion. The revised ranges may prove achievable, but the year had not ended as of the Q3 release. You can credit management for raising the range as operating results improved while still reserving judgment on the final annual result. And because 2026 GAAP earnings were distorted by unfavorable derivative fair values, the operational thesis should be tested with cargoes, volumes, contract margins and cash—not with one adjusted line alone. [3][9]

The 20/20 Vision milestone is a useful example of a commitment that can be checked against a dated outcome. Cheniere said it completed the plan nearly a year ahead of schedule and had deployed more than $20 billion since its 2022 announcement. That supports a view that the company can execute a multi-year capital program. It does not establish that every repurchase or construction dollar was equally productive, which is why you still compare growth investment, debt repayment, dividends and equity purchases with later operating cash. [3][11]

You should also judge the tone of a management statement against what it does and does not promise. Fusco's third-quarter comment linked the completed Stage 3 project and debottlenecking to better visibility into the initial 2027 production forecast. That is a clear operating thesis, but visibility is not the same as a delivered annual result. The next test will be cargoes, realized volumes, reliability and cash from the larger platform, not the confidence of the forecast alone. [3]

I would also separate actual results from the confidence embedded in an executive forecast. A guidance increase can reflect better completed operations, higher recognized volumes, improved margins, derivative normalization or several of these together. In Q3 2026 management cited higher delivered volumes and margins for improved Adjusted EBITDA, but the same nine-month period still had a GAAP derivative headwind. The test at year-end is whether audited operating cash and cash distributions support the updated range, not whether an interim presentation sounded persuasive. [3]

When you review the next expansion, insist on an evidence ledger. Record the date of the original schedule, the contractual guaranteed schedule, each train's first LNG and substantial-completion dates, the disclosed project cost status, customer contracts, export approvals and financing conditions. Cheniere's CCL Stage 3 history provides a favorable completed observation; CCL 8&9 and SPL Expansion remain work in progress. This prevents management's project pipeline from being mistaken for current production and gives you a fair basis to judge the next milestone when it arrives. [2][3][20][10]

Use a second ledger for financial promises. In 2026 management raised Adjusted EBITDA and DCF guidance after the first two quarters and raised them again in the third quarter. That upward movement accompanied higher volume and delivered margins, but it was not yet a full-year audited result, and the non-GAAP bridge included adjustments for derivatives and noncontrolling interests. A fair walk-the-talk audit can recognize better interim operating results while leaving the final annual test open. [3][9]

The call's CEO and CFO remarks are useful precisely because they separate evidence from expectation. Fusco said CCL Stage 3 completion provided 'increased visibility into our initial production forecast for 2027'; Davis said the first Sabine expansion phase was 'well positioned to reach FID' after final regulatory approvals. The first statement follows a completed handover; the second remains conditional. You should give each the weight its verb and gate deserve. [3][8]

The 2027 production outlook adds a measurable test after Stage 3. Management described 56–58 million tonnes of production, about 52 million tonnes under long-term agreements, roughly 5 million tonnes of spot capacity and 1 million tonnes still unsold at the October call. Those are preliminary commercial and production estimates, not audited results or full-year financial guidance. When the next report arrives, compare loaded volume, in-transit cargoes and cash conversion with each part of that plan. [8]

book_subsections.title: Capacity runway is gated, not additive
paragraphs: At the end of Q3 2026, management described approximately 56 mtpa operating, approximately 5 mtpa under construction or commissioning and more than 40 mtpa in permitting. You should keep three separate columns in your mind. Operating trains produce now. Construction trains require execution and commissioning. Permitted or pending projects require commercial and financing decisions as well as regulatory approvals. Adding all three gives a misleading picture of current capacity because they are not at the same stage of certainty. [3][20]

The most useful leading indicators therefore combine volumes, schedule, customer coverage, gas access and funding. Cargoes and TBtu show realized activity. Contract coverage indicates whether a future train has commercial purpose. Construction completion, permits and FID show whether the project is moving through its gates. Receivable and contract-asset aging reveal whether the accounting sale is becoming cash. The data set is incomplete—there is no public standardized DSO or train-utilization series here—but the missing observations should be named, not silently supplied. [2][3]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The promise I would test first is the one with a physical finish line. CCL Stage 3 now has one: the final train reached substantial completion on a dated milestone. Future capacity is different. A signed SPA, a FERC filing, a lender commitment or a construction percentage each advances the story, but none alone is an operating train. Give management credit for completed work and keep the unfinished work in the future tense.
